claim: Centrosomes organize spindle poles during mitosis.
source: While centrosomes organize spindle poles during mitosis, oocyte meiosis can occur in their absence.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology stated in the abstract.

claim: Oocyte meiosis can occur in the absence of centrosomes.
source: While centrosomes organize spindle poles during mitosis, oocyte meiosis can occur in their absence.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a known biological phenomenon.

claim: Spindles in human oocytes frequently fail to maintain bipolarity.
source: Spindles in human oocytes frequently fail to maintain bipolarity and consequently undergo chromosome segregation errors, making it important to understand the mechanisms that promote acentrosomal spindle stability.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work in the introduction.

claim: Spindles in human oocytes that fail to maintain bipolarity undergo chromosome segregation errors.
source: Spindles in human oocytes frequently fail to maintain bipolarity and consequently undergo chromosome segregation errors, making it important to understand the mechanisms that promote acentrosomal spindle stability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: The auxin-inducible degron system has been optimized in Caenorhabditis elegans for this study.
source: To this end, we have optimized the auxin-inducible degron system in Caenorhabditis elegans to remove the factors from pre-formed oocyte spindles within minutes and assess the effects on spindle structure.
evidence: The authors describe their methodological approach in the abstract.

claim: The optimized auxin-inducible degron system can remove factors from pre-formed oocyte spindles within minutes.
source: To this end, we have optimized the auxin-inducible degron system in Caenorhabditis elegans to remove the factors from pre-formed oocyte spindles within minutes and assess the effects on spindle structure.
evidence: This is a key methodological claim supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dynein is required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles.
source: This approach revealed that dynein is required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles; removal of dynein from bipolar spindles caused pole splaying, and when coupled with a monopolar spindle induced by depletion of the kinesin-12 motor KLP-18, dynein depletion led to a complete dissolution of the monopole.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Removal of dynein from bipolar spindles causes pole splaying.
source: This approach revealed that dynein is required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles; removal of dynein from bipolar spindles caused pole splaying, and when coupled with a monopolar spindle induced by depletion of the kinesin-12 motor KLP-18, dynein depletion led to a complete dissolution of the monopole.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claim: Depletion of the kinesin-12 motor KLP-18 induces a monopolar spindle.
source: This approach revealed that dynein is required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles; removal of dynein from bipolar spindles caused pole splaying, and when coupled with a monopolar spindle induced by depletion of the kinesin-12 motor KLP-18, dynein depletion led to a complete dissolution of the monopole.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior citations and experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Dynein depletion coupled with KLP-18 depletion leads to complete dissolution of the monopole.
source: This approach revealed that dynein is required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles; removal of dynein from bipolar spindles caused pole splaying, and when coupled with a monopolar spindle induced by depletion of the kinesin-12 motor KLP-18, dynein depletion led to a complete dissolution of the monopole.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3.

claim: Following monopole disruption, individual chromosomes can reorganize local microtubules and re-establish a miniature bipolar spindle.
source: Surprisingly, we went on to discover that following monopole disruption, individual chromosomes were able to reorganize local microtubules and re-establish a miniature bipolar spindle that mediated chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Miniature bipolar spindles formed after monopole disruption can mediate chromosome segregation.
source: Surprisingly, we went on to discover that following monopole disruption, individual chromosomes were able to reorganize local microtubules and re-establish a miniature bipolar spindle that mediated chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The formation of miniature bipolar spindles reveals the existence of redundant microtubule sorting forces.
source: This revealed the existence of redundant microtubule sorting forces that are undetectable when KLP-18 and dynein are active.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Redundant microtubule sorting forces are undetectable when KLP-18 and dynein are active.
source: This revealed the existence of redundant microtubule sorting forces that are undetectable when KLP-18 and dynein are active.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The kinesin-5 family motor BMK-1 provides microtubule sorting force in the absence of KLP-18 and dynein.
source: We found that the kinesin-5 family motor BMK-1 provides this force, uncovering the first evidence that kinesin-5 contributes to C. elegans meiotic spindle organization.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7.

claim: This study provides the first evidence that kinesin-5 contributes to C. elegans meiotic spindle organization.
source: We found that the kinesin-5 family motor BMK-1 provides this force, uncovering the first evidence that kinesin-5 contributes to C. elegans meiotic spindle organization.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Multiple motors work synchronously to establish and maintain bipolarity in the absence of centrosomes.
source: Altogether, our studies have revealed how multiple motors are working synchronously to establish and maintain bipolarity in the absence of centrosomes.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion of the study based on all experimental findings.

claim: Acentrosomal spindles in human oocytes are sometimes highly unstable.
source: In human oocytes, it has been shown that acentrosomal spindles are sometimes highly unstable; poles go through an extended period where they can split apart and then come back together, and spindles that display this instability have a high incidence of chromosome segregation errors (Holubcová et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holubcová et al., 2015.

claim: Poles of acentrosomal spindles in human oocytes can split apart and then come back together.
source: In human oocytes, it has been shown that acentrosomal spindles are sometimes highly unstable; poles go through an extended period where they can split apart and then come back together, and spindles that display this instability have a high incidence of chromosome segregation errors (Holubcová et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holubcová et al., 2015.

claim: Spindles in human oocytes that display instability have a high incidence of chromosome segregation errors.
source: In human oocytes, it has been shown that acentrosomal spindles are sometimes highly unstable; poles go through an extended period where they can split apart and then come back together, and spindles that display this instability have a high incidence of chromosome segregation errors (Holubcová et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holubcová et al., 2015.

claim: In C. elegans oocytes, microtubules are nucleated in proximity to the disassembling nuclear envelope in a spherical cage-like structure.
source: In C. elegans oocytes, microtubules are nucleated in proximity to the disassembling nuclear envelope in a spherical cage-like structure.
evidence: This is a description of the known process of spindle assembly in C. elegans oocytes, supported by citations.

claim: Microtubule minus ends are pushed outward to the periphery of the array by the kinesin-12 family motor KLP-18.
source: Microtubule minus ends are then pushed outward to the periphery of the array by the kinesin-12 family motor KLP-18, where they form multiple poles with clearly defined clusters of minus ends.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wolff et al., 2016 and Gigant et al., 2017.

claim: Microtubule minus ends form multiple poles with clearly defined clusters of minus ends.
source: Microtubule minus ends are then pushed outward to the periphery of the array by the kinesin-12 family motor KLP-18, where they form multiple poles with clearly defined clusters of minus ends.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wolff et al., 2016 and Gigant et al., 2017.

claim: Spindle poles coalesce to eventually form a bipolar structure with aligned chromosomes.
source: Spindle poles then coalesce, eventually forming a bipolar structure with aligned chromosomes (Wolff et al., 2016; Gigant et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wolff et al., 2016 and Gigant et al., 2017.

claim: Shortly after establishing a metaphase plate, the spindle shortens and rotates perpendicular to the cortex.
source: Shortly after establishing a metaphase plate, the spindle shortens and rotates perpendicular to the cortex and chromosomes begin to segregate in anaphase (Albertson and Thomson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Albertson and Thomson, 1993.

claim: Chromosomes begin to segregate in anaphase after the spindle rotates perpendicular to the cortex.
source: Shortly after establishing a metaphase plate, the spindle shortens and rotates perpendicular to the cortex and chromosomes begin to segregate in anaphase (Albertson and Thomson, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Albertson and Thomson, 1993.

claim: The cortical set of homologous chromosomes are discarded as a polar body.
source: The cortical set of homologous chromosomes are discarded as a polar body, and the remaining chromosomes undergo a second round of meiosis to generate the final set of maternal DNA.
evidence: This is a description of the known meiotic process in C. elegans oocytes.

claim: The remaining chromosomes undergo a second round of meiosis to generate the final set of maternal DNA.
source: The cortical set of homologous chromosomes are discarded as a polar body, and the remaining chromosomes undergo a second round of meiosis to generate the final set of maternal DNA.
evidence: This is a description of the known meiotic process in C. elegans oocytes.

claim: Many proteins that serve important functions in C. elegans mitotic spindle assembly can be found within acentrosomal meiotic spindles.
source: It would stand to reason that mitotic pole proteins are ideal candidates for also promoting meiotic pole stability; many proteins that serve important functions in C. elegans mitotic spindle assembly can be found within acentrosomal meiotic spindles (reviewed in Severson et al., 2016; Mullen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles by Severson et al., 2016 and Mullen et al., 2019.

claim: ASPM-1 concentrates at poles and contributes to acentrosomal spindle assembly.
source: Various microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) and microtubule motors have been demonstrated to concentrate at poles and contribute to acentrosomal spindle assembly, such as ASPM-1 (Connolly et al., 2014), KLP-7MCAK (Connolly et al., 2015; Han et al., 2015; Gigant et al., 2017), and MEI-1/2katanin (Srayko et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Connolly et al., 2014.

claim: KLP-7MCAK concentrates at poles and contributes to acentrosomal spindle assembly.
source: Various microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) and microtubule motors have been demonstrated to concentrate at poles and contribute to acentrosomal spindle assembly, such as ASPM-1 (Connolly et al., 2014), KLP-7MCAK (Connolly et al., 2015; Han et al., 2015; Gigant et al., 2017), and MEI-1/2katanin (Srayko et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Connolly et al., 2015; Han et al., 2015; and Gigant et al., 2017.

claim: MEI-1/2katanin concentrates at poles and contributes to acentrosomal spindle assembly.
source: Various microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) and microtubule motors have been demonstrated to concentrate at poles and contribute to acentrosomal spindle assembly, such as ASPM-1 (Connolly et al., 2014), KLP-7MCAK (Connolly et al., 2015; Han et al., 2015; Gigant et al., 2017), and MEI-1/2katanin (Srayko et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Srayko et al., 2000.

claim: Katanin is essential to maintain spindle structure.
source: A study using a fast-acting temperature-sensitive mei-1 mutant demonstrated that katanin is essential to maintain spindle structure (McNally et al., 2014), but whether any other pole-associated-proteins are required for spindle maintenance is not known.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McNally et al., 2014.

claim: Dynein is required for spindle pole focusing in mitotically dividing cells in multiple organisms.
source: Studies of mitotically dividing cells in multiple organisms have shown that dynein is required for spindle pole focusing and for centrosome anchoring to poles (reviewed in Borgal and Wakefield, 2018) and dynein also promotes poleward flux of newly formed microtubule minus ends (Elting et al., 2014; Hueschen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Borgal and Wakefield, 2018.

claim: Dynein is required for centrosome anchoring to poles in mitotically dividing cells.
source: Studies of mitotically dividing cells in multiple organisms have shown that dynein is required for spindle pole focusing and for centrosome anchoring to poles (reviewed in Borgal and Wakefield, 2018) and dynein also promotes poleward flux of newly formed microtubule minus ends (Elting et al., 2014; Hueschen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Borgal and Wakefield, 2018.

claim: Dynein promotes poleward flux of newly formed microtubule minus ends.
source: Studies of mitotically dividing cells in multiple organisms have shown that dynein is required for spindle pole focusing and for centrosome anchoring to poles (reviewed in Borgal and Wakefield, 2018) and dynein also promotes poleward flux of newly formed microtubule minus ends (Elting et al., 2014; Hueschen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elting et al., 2014 and Hueschen et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of dynein in Xenopus egg extracts creates broad, splayed acentrosomal spindle poles.
source: Inhibition of dynein in Xenopus egg extracts creates broad, splayed acentrosomal spindle poles (Heald et al., 1996), and injection of dynein antibodies into Xenopus oocytes disrupts overall meiotic spindle organization (Becker et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heald et al., 1996.

claim: Injection of dynein antibodies into Xenopus oocytes disrupts overall meiotic spindle organization.
source: Inhibition of dynein in Xenopus egg extracts creates broad, splayed acentrosomal spindle poles (Heald et al., 1996), and injection of dynein antibodies into Xenopus oocytes disrupts overall meiotic spindle organization (Becker et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Becker et al., 2003.

claim: In mouse oocytes, dynein is involved in the early stages of spindle assembly.
source: In mouse oocytes, dynein is involved in the early stages of spindle assembly, so dynein inhibition prevents spindle (and thus pole) formation entirely (Luksza et al., 2013; Clift and Schuh, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luksza et al., 2013 and Clift and Schuh, 2015.

claim: Dynein inhibition in mouse oocytes prevents spindle formation entirely.
source: In mouse oocytes, dynein is involved in the early stages of spindle assembly, so dynein inhibition prevents spindle (and thus pole) formation entirely (Luksza et al., 2013; Clift and Schuh, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luksza et al., 2013 and Clift and Schuh, 2015.

claim: In C. elegans, dynein is crucial for the proper positioning of both mitotic and meiotic spindles.
source: In C. elegans, dynein is crucial for the proper positioning of both mitotic and meiotic spindles, and for spindle rotation during meiotic anaphase (Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; and Crowder et al., 2015.

claim: In C. elegans, dynein is crucial for spindle rotation during meiotic anaphase.
source: In C. elegans, dynein is crucial for the proper positioning of both mitotic and meiotic spindles, and for spindle rotation during meiotic anaphase (Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; and Crowder et al., 2015.

claim: Depletion of dynein or its cofactor dynactin causes spindle defects in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Moreover, a number of studies have shown that depletion of dynein or its cofactor dynactin causes spindle defects in oocytes, such as longer spindles with pole defects (Yang et al., 2005; Ellefson and McNally, 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015; Muscat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2005; Ellefson and McNally, 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015; and Muscat et al., 2015.

claim: Depletion of dynein or dynactin causes longer spindles with pole defects in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Moreover, a number of studies have shown that depletion of dynein or its cofactor dynactin causes spindle defects in oocytes, such as longer spindles with pole defects (Yang et al., 2005; Ellefson and McNally, 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015; Muscat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2005; Ellefson and McNally, 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015; and Muscat et al., 2015.

claim: The Dynein AID strain appears superficially wild type with no noticeable effects on worm development, brood size, or percent of male progeny in the absence of auxin.
source: This strain appears superficially wild type, with no noticeable effects on worm development, brood size, or percent of male progeny, suggesting that the GFP and degron tags are not affecting dynein function in the absence of auxin (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015 and observation.

claim: The GFP and degron tags are not affecting dynein function in the absence of auxin.
source: This strain appears superficially wild type, with no noticeable effects on worm development, brood size, or percent of male progeny, suggesting that the GFP and degron tags are not affecting dynein function in the absence of auxin (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the strain appears wild type.

claim: After 4 hr incubation of adult Dynein AID worms on auxin-containing plates, clear defects in centrosome separation and spindle positioning along the A-P axis were observed in mitotic embryos.
source: After a 4 hr incubation of adult Dynein AID worms on auxin-containing plates, we observed clear defects in centrosome separation and spindle positioning along the A-P axis and dynein was undetectable (22/22 mitotic embryos) (Figure 1B), confirming strong depletion in embryos under conditions where germline and worm development are not affected.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dynein was undetectable in 22/22 mitotic embryos after 4 hr auxin treatment.
source: After a 4 hr incubation of adult Dynein AID worms on auxin-containing plates, we observed clear defects in centrosome separation and spindle positioning along the A-P axis and dynein was undetectable (22/22 mitotic embryos) (Figure 1B), confirming strong depletion in embryos under conditions where germline and worm development are not affected.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dynein is localized to the spindle in C. elegans oocytes, with increasing enrichment at acentrosomal poles at the anaphase transition.
source: To further validate the Dynein AID strain, we assessed the localization of tagged dynein throughout oocyte meiosis and found that the pattern was consistent with previous studies (Figure 1C; Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015). Dynein was weakly associated with forming and bipolar spindles with a slight enrichment at acentrosomal poles, labeled by the microtubule minus end marker ASPM-1, and then became strongly enriched at poles during early anaphase; this enrichment decreased by late anaphase, with a population that was retained near the cortex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: Dynein enrichment at poles decreases by late anaphase, with a population retained near the cortex.
source: Dynein was weakly associated with forming and bipolar spindles with a slight enrichment at acentrosomal poles, labeled by the microtubule minus end marker ASPM-1, and then became strongly enriched at poles during early anaphase; this enrichment decreased by late anaphase, with a population that was retained near the cortex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Live imaging corroborated the fixed imaging of dynein localization.
source: Live imaging corroborated our fixed imaging (Video 1, n = 3) and also made clearer a population of dynein at kinetochores, as has been shown in other live imaging studies (McNally et al., 2016; Danlasky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by Video 1 and citations to McNally et al., 2016 and Danlasky et al., 2020.

claim: A population of dynein localizes at kinetochores.
source: Live imaging corroborated our fixed imaging (Video 1, n = 3) and also made clearer a population of dynein at kinetochores, as has been shown in other live imaging studies (McNally et al., 2016; Danlasky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown in Video 1 and supported by citations to McNally et al., 2016 and Danlasky et al., 2020.

claim: Following 4 hr of auxin treatment, most spindles in the Dynein AID strain had splayed poles (84/121, 69.4%).
source: However, following 4 hr of auxin treatment, most spindles had splayed poles; a majority of spindles displayed microtubule bundles that did not come together at a single focused point on either side of the chromosomes (84/121, 69.4%), similar to what was observed following depletion of dynactin component DNC-1 in a previous study (Crowder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: Imaging of ASPM-1 confirmed the pole splaying phenotype at a percentage similar to that observed using germline counting (39/54, 72.2%).
source: Imaging of ASPM-1 confirmed this phenotype at a percentage similar to that observed using germline counting (39/54, 72.2%); following a 4 hr auxin treatment, microtubule minus ends lacked coalesced points between the ends of microtubule bundles (Figure 1E and F, Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1E, F and Table 2.

claim: Following 4 hr auxin treatment, microtubule minus ends lacked coalesced points between the ends of microtubule bundles.
source: Imaging of ASPM-1 confirmed this phenotype at a percentage similar to that observed using germline counting (39/54, 72.2%); following a 4 hr auxin treatment, microtubule minus ends lacked coalesced points between the ends of microtubule bundles (Figure 1E and F, Table 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1E, F and Table 2.

claim: Defects in spindle rotation were observed following dynein depletion.
source: Moreover, we also saw defects in spindle rotation in anaphase (Figure 1D and E), consistent with previous studies (Ellefson and McNally, 2009; van der Voet et al., 2009; Ellefson and McNally, 2011; Crowder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and E and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: In the TIR1 control strain, there was no significant difference between control and auxin-treated worms at any position in the germline.
source: To confirm that these defects were not caused by nonspecific effects of auxin, we performed germline counting in a 'TIR1 control' strain that contained all of the same transgenes but lacked degron-tagged DHC-1. In this strain, there was no significant difference between control and auxin-treated worms at any position in the germline, and all stages of spindle assembly appeared identical (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 3).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 3.

claim: The frequency of pole splaying was nearly identical between lin-5(RNAi), aspm-1(RNAi), and long-term Dynein AID.
source: The frequency of pole splaying was nearly identical between these two RNAi conditions and long-term Dynein AID (167/261, 64%, and 364/521, 69.9%, for the +1 position in lin-5 and aspm-1 RNAi, respectively, compared to 84/121, 69.4% for Dynein AID); this quantification was in agreement with previous observations of spindle morphology following aspm-1(RNAi) or lin-5(RNAi) (van der Voet et al., 2009; Wignall and Villeneuve, 2009; Connolly et al., 2014; Laband et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Table 4.

claim: Treatment with auxin to remove dynein did not exacerbate the pole defects of either aspm-1(RNAi) or lin-5(RNAi).
source: To determine if the pole splaying observed following LIN-5 and ASPM-1 depletion was mostly a consequence of dynein mislocalization, we combined these RNAi conditions with Dynein AID depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). Treatment with auxin to remove dynein did not exacerbate the pole defects of either aspm-1(RNAi) or lin-5(RNAi), nor present any new phenotypes that were not present in the RNAi conditions alone, except for removing the kinetochore population of dynein (pole defects were consistent in 37/37 lin-5(RNAi) and 56/56 aspm-1(RNAi) oocyte spindles treated with auxin).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Dynein's localization to poles is necessary for its role in pole coalescence during spindle assembly.
source: These results confirm that dynein's localization to poles is necessary for its role in pole coalescence during spindle assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings with lin-5(RNAi) and aspm-1(RNAi).

claim: Short-term dynein depletion from metaphase-arrested spindles caused nearly all spindles to have severely splayed poles.
source: We therefore arrested oocytes in metaphase I to enrich for pre-formed spindles (by depleting anaphase-promoting complex component EMB-30; Furuta et al., 2000), soaked worms in auxin for 25–30 min to deplete dynein, and then performed IF. Under these conditions, nearly all spindles had severely splayed poles (Figure 2A and B); we measured the widths of the spindle equator and the poles and found an approximately 50% increase in the pole to equator ratio upon auxin treatment.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There was an approximately 50% increase in the pole to equator ratio upon auxin treatment in short-term dynein depletion.
source: Under these conditions, nearly all spindles had severely splayed poles (Figure 2A and B); we measured the widths of the spindle equator and the poles and found an approximately 50% increase in the pole to equator ratio upon auxin treatment.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Despite pole splaying after short-term dynein depletion, microtubule bundles retained lateral associations with the chromosomes.
source: Despite this pole splaying, microtubule bundles retained lateral associations with the chromosomes, resulting in a spindle that was still bipolar but more rectangular than wild-type spindles.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pole splaying phenotype was observed in the absence of emb-30(RNAi), demonstrating that it is not dependent on the metaphase arrest.
source: Notably, we observed these same phenotypes in the absence of emb-30(RNAi), demonstrating that they are not dependent on the metaphase arrest (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ASPM-1 appeared more dispersed throughout the spindle following acute dynein depletion.
source: During this analysis, we also noticed that while ASPM-1 remained localized to dynein-depleted poles it appeared more dispersed throughout the spindle; this suggests a decrease in poleward transport of microtubule minus ends, as has been reported in dynein-depleted mitotic spindles (Hueschen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Acute dynein depletion suggests a decrease in poleward transport of microtubule minus ends.
source: During this analysis, we also noticed that while ASPM-1 remained localized to dynein-depleted poles it appeared more dispersed throughout the spindle; this suggests a decrease in poleward transport of microtubule minus ends, as has been reported in dynein-depleted mitotic spindles (Hueschen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ASPM-1 localization data and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Both unarrested and metaphase-arrested spindles were significantly longer (~3.5 μm) after short-term Dynein AID depletion.
source: Moreover, we also measured the pole-to-pole lengths of these spindles and found that both unarrested and metaphase-arrested spindles were significantly longer (~3.5 μm) after short-term Dynein AID depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dynein provides an inward force that maintains spindle length.
source: These data suggest that dynein not only promotes focusing of microtubule minus ends into discrete poles, but also provides an inward force that maintains spindle length.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spindle length measurements after dynein depletion.

claim: When oocytes were dissected into auxin, dynein appeared depleted from meiotic spindles within roughly 3 min.
source: In contrast, when oocytes were dissected into auxin, dynein appeared depleted from meiotic spindles within roughly 3 min and acentrosomal poles began to splay (Figure 2C, Video 3, n = 4).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2C and Video 3.

claim: Acentrosomal poles began to splay after dynein depletion in acute AID experiments.
source: In contrast, when oocytes were dissected into auxin, dynein appeared depleted from meiotic spindles within roughly 3 min and acentrosomal poles began to splay (Figure 2C, Video 3, n = 4).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2C and Video 3.

claim: Despite pole splaying and spindle lengthening after acute dynein depletion, microtubule bundles remained associated with chromosomes and the spindles maintained bipolarity.
source: As before, metaphase-arrested spindles were quickly disrupted upon dissection into auxin solution (Video 5, n = 8); poles began to splay (Figure 2D, arrowheads) and spindles again lengthened. Despite these changes, microtubule bundles were able to remain associated with chromosomes and the spindles maintained bipolarity.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2D and Video 5.

claim: Neither untreated nor auxin-treated TIR1 control oocytes exhibited significant changes to either spindle length or pole to equator ratio.
source: To ensure that these phenotypes were not caused by auxin itself having nonspecific effects on dissected oocytes, we performed analogous live imaging experiments in our TIR1 control strain (lacking degron-tagged DHC-1) to assess the effects of auxin treatment in the absence of dynein depletion. Neither untreated nor auxin-treated oocytes exhibited significant changes to either spindle length or pole to equator ratio (n = 5 for each condition); we compared both individual traces and average change from baseline for both of these parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Videos 6 and 7.

claim: Auxin-treated oocytes progressed through anaphase despite pole splaying, albeit with lagging chromosomes.
source: Additionally, we repeated these experiments without emb-30(RNAi) and saw the same pole defects in the absence of the metaphase arrest (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Videos 8–11). These auxin-treated oocytes progressed through anaphase despite pole splaying, albeit with lagging chromosomes, as has been observed previously following dynein depletion (Muscat et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Videos 8–11, and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: Dynein is required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles once they have been established.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that dynein is not only required to focus poles during meiotic spindle assembly, but is also required to maintain the integrity of acentrosomal poles once they have been established.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings from acute dynein depletion experiments.

claim: Oocytes from klp-18(RNAi) worms treated with long-term Dynein AID rarely displayed a monopolar spindle.
source: First, we performed long-term Dynein AID in worms treated with klp-18(RNAi) and found that oocytes from these worms rarely displayed a monopolar spindle (Figure 3A, Table 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3A and Table 5.

claim: Following long-term Dynein AID in klp-18(RNAi) worms, oocyte chromosomes were dispersed, retaining lateral associations to microtubule bundles (116/125 in the +1 position, 92.8%).
source: Instead, oocyte chromosomes were dispersed, retaining lateral associations to microtubule bundles (116/125 in the +1 position, 92.8%).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3A and Table 5.

claim: IF imaging following short-term AID treatment in klp-18(RNAi) confirmed that monopoles had begun breaking apart, ejecting chromosomes and associated microtubule bundles into the cytoplasm.
source: IF imaging following short-term AID treatment confirmed this result; ASPM-1 labeling revealed that monopoles had begun breaking apart, ejecting chromosomes and associated microtubule bundles into the cytoplasm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In some cases following monopole breakdown, the entirety of the monopole disappeared, and each chromosome retained its own associated microtubule bundles.
source: In some cases, the entirety of the monopole disappeared, and each chromosome retained its own associated microtubule bundles.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Many chromosome-associated microtubule structures following monopole breakdown had a distinct cone shape, with microtubule ends focused on one side of the chromosome and splayed on the other side.
source: Many of these structures had a distinct cone shape, with microtubule ends focused on one side of the chromosome and splayed on the other side (Figure 3B, zooms); we speculate that the microtubule minus ends are coalesced together at the pointy end of this structure, retaining some association even after they were released from the monopole upon spindle breakdown.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The microtubule minus ends are coalesced together at the pointy end of the cone-shaped structures following monopole breakdown.
source: Many of these structures had a distinct cone shape, with microtubule ends focused on one side of the chromosome and splayed on the other side (Figure 3B, zooms); we speculate that the microtubule minus ends are coalesced together at the pointy end of this structure, retaining some association even after they were released from the monopole upon spindle breakdown.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed cone shape.

claim: Acute dynein depletion from monopolar spindles led to rapid breakdown of the monopole.
source: We observed the same phenotype using acute dynein depletion coupled with live ex utero imaging; when oocytes containing monopolar spindles were dissected into auxin, we observed rapid breakdown of the monopole on a timescale similar to that required for dynein depletion from bipolar spindles (Figure 4A and B, Video 12 and Video 13, n = 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4A, B and Videos 12 and 13.

claim: As the monopolar spindle began to fragment, microtubule bundles remained associated with individual chromosomes via lateral associations.
source: As the monopolar spindle began to fragment, microtubule bundles remained associated with individual chromosomes via lateral associations (Figure 4A, arrowheads), as seen in fixed imaging (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dynein has an essential role in maintaining pole integrity.
source: These results demonstrate an essential role for dynein in maintaining pole integrity and suggest that in the case of dynein depletion from bipolar spindles the intact overlap zone stabilizes the spindle even though poles are completely disrupted.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the monopole breakdown experiments.

claim: In the case of dynein depletion from bipolar spindles, the intact overlap zone stabilizes the spindle even though poles are completely disrupted.
source: These results demonstrate an essential role for dynein in maintaining pole integrity and suggest that in the case of dynein depletion from bipolar spindles the intact overlap zone stabilizes the spindle even though poles are completely disrupted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of bipolar and monopolar spindle phenotypes after dynein depletion.

claim: In the absence of auxin, chromosomes extended outward from the monopole towards microtubule plus ends, and then moved back towards the monopole during anaphase.
source: These experiments were not done using metaphase arrest, so in the absence of auxin, chromosomes extended outward from the monopole towards microtubule plus ends, and then moved back towards the monopole during anaphase (Figure 4A, Video 14, n = 6), as has been described previously (Muscat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Video 14, and is consistent with previous work cited.

claim: Following breakdown of the monopole after acute dynein depletion, each individual chromosome began to segregate.
source: In auxin-treated oocytes, as filming continued past the full breakdown of the monopole, we were surprised to see that each individual chromosome began to segregate (Figure 4A and B, Videos 12 and 13, n = 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4A, B and Videos 12 and 13.

claim: Segregation of individual chromosomes following monopole breakdown occurred synchronously across the oocyte.
source: This segregation was incredibly striking as it occurred synchronously across the oocyte and each set of separating chromosomes exhibited distinct bidirectional movement, reminiscent of normal chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and Videos 12 and 13.

claim: Each set of separating chromosomes following monopole breakdown exhibited distinct bidirectional movement, reminiscent of normal chromosome segregation.
source: This segregation was incredibly striking as it occurred synchronously across the oocyte and each set of separating chromosomes exhibited distinct bidirectional movement, reminiscent of normal chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and Videos 12 and 13.

claim: Neither KLP-18 nor dynein is absolutely required for chromosome segregation in oocytes.
source: The fact that we observed these anaphase-like movements in the absence of both KLP-18 and dynein suggests that neither motor is absolutely required for chromosome segregation in oocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of chromosome segregation in the absence of both motors.

claim: Chromosomes on dynein-depleted klp-18(RNAi) mini anaphase spindles segregated to a similar final distance as wild-type spindles (~5 µm for both).
source: To assess whether these segregations were similar to normal anaphases, we first quantified the segregation distances of individual chromosomes and compared them to both wild-type and dynein-depleted anaphases (Figure 4C). Chromosomes on dynein-depleted klp-18(RNAi) mini anaphase spindles segregated to a similar final distance as wild-type spindles (~5 µm for both wild-type and mini anaphases).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mini anaphases did not appear to segregate as far as dynein-depleted bipolar anaphases, where KLP-18 was not depleted (~6.5 µm).
source: However, mini anaphases did not appear to segregate as far as dynein-depleted bipolar anaphases, where KLP-18 was not depleted (~6.5 µm).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 4C.

claim: KLP-18 may normally contribute to anaphase spindle elongation through microtubule sliding.
source: This observation raises the possibility that, even though chromosomes can segregate without KLP-18, this motor may normally contribute to anaphase spindle elongation through microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is speculation based on the segregation distance measurements.

claim: Mini anaphases have key hallmarks of normal anaphase spindles.
source: To further characterize these segregations, we performed fixed imaging to generate higher-resolution images. This analysis revealed that the mini anaphases have key hallmarks of normal anaphase spindles; when chromosomes were still close together, we observed lateral microtubule bundles running alongside the separating chromosomes (Figure 5, 'early anaphase'), and as chromosomes segregated further and spindle length increased, microtubules were largely localized between chromosomes (Figure 5, 'late anaphase').
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5.

claim: In early mini anaphases, lateral microtubule bundles run alongside the separating chromosomes.
source: This analysis revealed that the mini anaphases have key hallmarks of normal anaphase spindles; when chromosomes were still close together, we observed lateral microtubule bundles running alongside the separating chromosomes (Figure 5, 'early anaphase'), and as chromosomes segregated further and spindle length increased, microtubules were largely localized between chromosomes (Figure 5, 'late anaphase').
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5.

claim: In late mini anaphases, microtubules are largely localized between chromosomes.
source: This analysis revealed that the mini anaphases have key hallmarks of normal anaphase spindles; when chromosomes were still close together, we observed lateral microtubule bundles running alongside the separating chromosomes (Figure 5, 'early anaphase'), and as chromosomes segregated further and spindle length increased, microtubules were largely localized between chromosomes (Figure 5, 'late anaphase').
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mini spindles undergo morphological changes and anaphase-B-like spindle elongation as they drive chromosomes apart.
source: This suggests that, like normal anaphase spindles, these mini spindles undergo morphological changes and anaphase-B-like spindle elongation as they drive chromosomes apart.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed microtubule localization patterns in mini anaphases.

claim: SUMO-marked RCs were removed from chromosomes during anaphase and remained between segregating chromosomes in control and dynein depletion conditions.
source: To assess RC behavior, we imaged SUMO, a post-translational modification found in the RC (Pelisch et al., 2017). In control and dynein depletion conditions, SUMO-marked RCs were removed from chromosomes during anaphase and remained between segregating chromosomes, as expected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: During monopolar spindle breakdown, SUMO localized to RCs as individual chromosomes detached from the dissolving monopole.
source: During monopolar spindle breakdown, SUMO localized to RCs as individual chromosomes detached from the dissolving monopole.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In mini anaphases, SUMO marked a singular disassembling RC between each segregating chromosome pair (93/93 oocytes observed).
source: In mini anaphases, SUMO marked a singular disassembling RC between each segregating chromosome pair (93/93 oocytes observed), congruent with the normal behavior of RCs in anaphase.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SEP-1 (separase) is a protease that cleaves a component of the cohesin complex, enabling homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) and sister chromatids (meiosis II) to separate.
source: Next, we assessed SEP-1 (separase), a protease that cleaves a component of the cohesin complex, enabling homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) and sister chromatids (meiosis II) to separate (Siomos et al., 2001; Kudo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Siomos et al., 2001 and Kudo et al., 2006.

claim: During wild-type meiosis, SEP-1 localizes to kinetochores in metaphase and relocalizes to RCs at anaphase onset.
source: During wild-type meiosis, SEP-1 localizes to kinetochores in metaphase and relocalizes to RCs at anaphase onset; by the end of anaphase, SEP-1 is no longer detectable on the anaphase spindle (Muscat et al., 2015; Davis-Roca et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muscat et al., 2015 and Davis-Roca et al., 2017.

claim: By the end of anaphase, SEP-1 is no longer detectable on the anaphase spindle.
source: During wild-type meiosis, SEP-1 localizes to kinetochores in metaphase and relocalizes to RCs at anaphase onset; by the end of anaphase, SEP-1 is no longer detectable on the anaphase spindle (Muscat et al., 2015; Davis-Roca et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muscat et al., 2015 and Davis-Roca et al., 2017.

claim: After monopole breakdown, SEP-1 relocalized from kinetochores to RCs, and then was absent from each mini spindle in late anaphase (81/81 oocytes observed).
source: We observed this same pattern when assessing monopolar breakdowns following klp-18(RNAi) and short-term Dynein AID. After monopole breakdown, SEP-1 relocalized from kinetochores to RCs, and then was absent from each mini spindle in late anaphase (81/81 oocytes observed) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Miniature spindles recapitulate the key aspects of normal anaphase progression.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that miniature spindles recapitulate the key aspects of normal anaphase progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the SUMO and SEP-1 localization data.

claim: Some local microtubule reorganization must be occurring after monopole breakdown to enable bidirectional chromosome movement.
source: The fact that we observed chromosome segregation with hallmarks of normal anaphase led us to hypothesize that some local microtubule reorganization must be occurring after monopole breakdown; without a bipolar distribution of microtubule minus ends, it should not be possible for chromosomes to move away from each other in the manner we observed.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed chromosome segregation.

claim: Microtubules may reorganize into a bipolar structure around each chromosome following monopole breakdown.
source: Therefore, while all microtubule minus ends are together in the monopole before dynein depletion, we speculated that these microtubules may reorganize into a bipolar structure around each chromosome following monopole breakdown.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed chromosome segregation.

claim: ASPM-1 could be seen on both sides of mini spindles during a transitional period, with minor enrichment towards areas resembling spindle poles (n = 3 oocytes).
source: In order to better characterize this possible reorganization, we assessed the localization of ASPM-1 as a marker of microtubule minus ends. On a few occasions (n = 3 oocytes), we were able to capture what appeared to be a transitional period, indicating that reorganization was occurring; ASPM-1 could be seen on both sides of these mini spindles, with minor enrichment towards areas resembling spindle poles (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SPD-1 localizes to the anaphase spindle midzone in oocytes, marking a region of antiparallel microtubule overlap.
source: To test this idea, we assessed the localization of a well-studied spindle protein, the PRC1 homolog SPD-1. SPD-1 localizes to the anaphase spindle midzone in oocytes, marking a region of antiparallel microtubule overlap (Hattersley et al., 2016; Gigant et al., 2017; Mullen et al., 2017; Figure 6B, row 2), and we found that SPD-1 was also at this location in the absence of dynein (Figure 6B, row 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and is supported by citations to Hattersley et al., 2016; Gigant et al., 2017; and Mullen et al., 2017.

claim: SPD-1 was at the anaphase spindle midzone in the absence of dynein.
source: SPD-1 localizes to the anaphase spindle midzone in oocytes, marking a region of antiparallel microtubule overlap (Hattersley et al., 2016; Gigant et al., 2017; Mullen et al., 2017; Figure 6B, row 2), and we found that SPD-1 was also at this location in the absence of dynein (Figure 6B, row 4).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In intact and disassembling monopoles, SPD-1 was not localized to microtubules as it only associates with the spindle in anaphase.
source: In intact and disassembling monopoles, SPD-1 was not localized to microtubules as it only associates with the spindle in anaphase.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Once chromosomes had been ejected into the cytoplasm, SPD-1 could be clearly observed between segregating chromosomes (122/122 oocytes observed).
source: However, once chromosomes had been ejected into the cytoplasm, SPD-1 could be clearly observed between segregating chromosomes (Figure 6B, bottom row, 122/122 oocytes observed), demonstrating that the mini anaphase spindles have a region of antiparallel microtubule overlap in the center.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The mini anaphase spindles have a region of antiparallel microtubule overlap in the center.
source: However, once chromosomes had been ejected into the cytoplasm, SPD-1 could be clearly observed between segregating chromosomes (Figure 6B, bottom row, 122/122 oocytes observed), demonstrating that the mini anaphase spindles have a region of antiparallel microtubule overlap in the center.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the SPD-1 localization data.

claim: The discovery that microtubules reorganize around dispersed chromosomes suggests the presence of an activity that can sort microtubules and re-establish bipolarity in the absence of KLP-18 and dynein.
source: Our discovery that microtubules were able to reorganize around dispersed chromosomes and establish a region of antiparallel overlap at the center of each mini spindle suggested the presence of an activity that can sort microtubules and re-establish bipolarity in the absence of KLP-18 and dynein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: This condition provides a unique opportunity to probe for redundant motor forces that may be present in a normal meiotic spindle, but would otherwise be masked by the presence of the forces provided by KLP-18 and dynein.
source: We saw this condition as a unique opportunity to probe for redundant motor forces that may be present in a normal meiotic spindle, but would otherwise be masked by the presence of the forces provided by KLP-18 and dynein.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental rationale.

claim: BMK-1 is the sole kinesin-5 family motor in C. elegans.
source: One strong candidate was the sole kinesin-5 family motor in C. elegans, BMK-1 (Bishop et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bishop et al., 2005.

claim: Kinesin-5 motors have essential roles in establishing spindle bipolarity in many organisms.
source: Kinesin-5 motors have essential roles in establishing spindle bipolarity in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019), but loss of BMK-1 has not been reported to have major phenotypes in C. elegans; BMK-1 depletion has no effects on spindle morphology in either oocytes or embryos (Bishop et al., 2005) and only minor effects on chromosome segregation rates (Saunders et al., 2007; Laband et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Mann and Wadsworth, 2019.

claim: Loss of BMK-1 has not been reported to have major phenotypes in C. elegans.
source: Kinesin-5 motors have essential roles in establishing spindle bipolarity in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019), but loss of BMK-1 has not been reported to have major phenotypes in C. elegans; BMK-1 depletion has no effects on spindle morphology in either oocytes or embryos (Bishop et al., 2005) and only minor effects on chromosome segregation rates (Saunders et al., 2007; Laband et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bishop et al., 2005; Saunders et al., 2007; and Laband et al., 2017.

claim: BMK-1 depletion has no effects on spindle morphology in either oocytes or embryos.
source: Kinesin-5 motors have essential roles in establishing spindle bipolarity in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019), but loss of BMK-1 has not been reported to have major phenotypes in C. elegans; BMK-1 depletion has no effects on spindle morphology in either oocytes or embryos (Bishop et al., 2005) and only minor effects on chromosome segregation rates (Saunders et al., 2007; Laband et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bishop et al., 2005.

claim: BMK-1 depletion has only minor effects on chromosome segregation rates.
source: Kinesin-5 motors have essential roles in establishing spindle bipolarity in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019), but loss of BMK-1 has not been reported to have major phenotypes in C. elegans; BMK-1 depletion has no effects on spindle morphology in either oocytes or embryos (Bishop et al., 2005) and only minor effects on chromosome segregation rates (Saunders et al., 2007; Laband et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saunders et al., 2007 and Laband et al., 2017.

claim: BMK-1 could be providing a supplementary outward sorting force that is normally masked by the contributions of KLP-18.
source: We therefore hypothesized that BMK-1 could be providing a supplementary outward sorting force that is normally masked by the contributions of KLP-18.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known roles of kinesin-5 motors in other organisms.

claim: BMK-1 was broadly associated with bipolar metaphase and anaphase spindles in both control and dynein-depletion conditions.
source: To probe this hypothesis, we first sought to confirm the localization of BMK-1 on meiotic spindles and to test if this motor was localized to microtubules under monopole breakdown conditions. BMK-1 was broadly associated with bipolar metaphase and anaphase spindles in both control and dynein-depletion conditions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In intact monopolar spindles, BMK-1 localized to microtubules.
source: In intact monopolar spindles, BMK-1 also localized to microtubules.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When dynein was depleted and monopole breakdown was induced, BMK-1 still localized to microtubules (150/150 oocytes observed).
source: Importantly, when we depleted dynein and induced monopole breakdown, BMK-1 still localized to microtubules (Figure 7A, zooms), placing it in a location where it could contribute to microtubule reorganization (150/150 oocytes observed).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Following monopolar spindle breakdown in the bmk-1(ok391) background, no mini anaphase spindles were observed (0/164 oocytes).
source: We then generated monopolar spindles, performed short-term Dynein AID, and performed IF in the bmk-1(ok391) background. Under these conditions, we were unable to observe any mini anaphase spindles (0/164 oocytes), even though monopole breakdown still occurred (Figure 7B and C, Table 6).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7B, C and Table 6.

claim: Monopole breakdown still occurred in the bmk-1(ok391) background following short-term Dynein AID.
source: Under these conditions, we were unable to observe any mini anaphase spindles (0/164 oocytes), even though monopole breakdown still occurred (Figure 7B and C, Table 6).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7B, C and Table 6.

claim: Removal of BMK-1 function abolished microtubule reorganization and prevented chromosome segregation following monopole breakdown.
source: This suggested that removal of BMK-1 function abolished microtubule reorganization and prevented chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of mini anaphases in the bmk-1(ok391) background.

claim: In klp-18(RNAi), bmk-1(syb3914) worms in the absence of auxin, monopolar spindles formed and then chromosomes moved back towards the pole in a manner indistinguishable from normal monopolar anaphase.
source: To confirm this result, we generated a version of our Dynein AID live imaging strain (expressing GFP::tubulin and GFP::histone to visualize the spindle) containing the bmk-1(syb3914) deletion and performed acute dynein depletion coupled with ex utero imaging to determine if mini anaphases could still form. In klp-18(RNAi), bmk-1(syb3914) worms in the absence of auxin, monopolar spindles formed and then chromosomes moved back towards the pole in a manner indistinguishable from normal monopolar anaphase (Video 15, n = 4).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Video 15.

claim: When auxin was added to deplete dynein in klp-18(RNAi), bmk-1(syb3914) worms, monopolar spindles broke down as expected and individual chromosomes remained associated with microtubule bundles, but there were no signs of segregation.
source: When auxin was added to deplete dynein, monopolar spindles broke down as expected and individual chromosomes remained associated with microtubule bundles. However, as time elapsed, there were no signs of segregation, microtubule density decreased, and chromosomes remained in the cytoplasm with no discernible anaphase spindles forming (Figure 7D, Video 16, n = 3).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7D and Video 16.

claim: BMK-1 provides outward sorting force on microtubules during oocyte meiosis, redundant to the forces produced by KLP-18.
source: These data support the hypothesis that BMK-1 provides outward sorting force on microtubules during oocyte meiosis, redundant to the forces produced by KLP-18.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings with bmk-1 mutants.

claim: Dynein activity is required throughout the meiotic divisions to establish and maintain focused poles.
source: Collectively, these data have contributed to a more complete model for how acentrosomal spindles are assembled and stabilized during oocyte meiosis (Figure 8). Dynein activity is required throughout the meiotic divisions to establish and maintain focused poles, and its removal via acute AID generated spindle defects within minutes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Removal of dynein via acute AID generated spindle defects within minutes.
source: Dynein activity is required throughout the meiotic divisions to establish and maintain focused poles, and its removal via acute AID generated spindle defects within minutes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from acute AID experiments.

claim: Dynein depletion increased the length of bipolar oocyte spindles.
source: Dynein depletion increased the length of bipolar oocyte spindles and led to increased dispersion of microtubule minus ends across the spindle.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dynein depletion led to increased dispersion of microtubule minus ends across the spindle.
source: Dynein depletion increased the length of bipolar oocyte spindles and led to increased dispersion of microtubule minus ends across the spindle.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When performing dynein depletions on a monopolar spindle, the monopole completely broke apart and microtubule bundles were ejected into the cytoplasm.
source: When performing these depletions on a monopolar spindle, the monopole completely broke apart and microtubule bundles were ejected into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Dynein is required to stitch minus ends together into a stable pole structure.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that dynein is required to stitch minus ends together into a stable pole structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the dynein depletion experiments.

claim: After the monopole disassembled, microtubules were able to reorganize into a 'miniature' spindle.
source: Remarkably, we also found that after the monopole disassembled, microtubules were able to reorganize into a 'miniature' spindle; chromosomes then segregated on these spindles in the absence of dynein.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Chromosomes segregated on miniature spindles in the absence of dynein.
source: Remarkably, we also found that after the monopole disassembled, microtubules were able to reorganize into a 'miniature' spindle; chromosomes then segregated on these spindles in the absence of dynein.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The finding that chromosomes segregate on miniature spindles seemingly contradicts a previous study where dynein was proposed to drive chromosomes towards poles along laterally associated microtubule bundles.
source: This finding seemingly contradicts one of our previous studies, where we proposed that dynein could drive chromosomes towards poles along laterally associated microtubule bundles, representing a type of 'anaphase A' segregation mechanism (Muscat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a discussion of how the current findings relate to previous work.

claim: Dynein was a good candidate for driving chromosomes towards poles since it provided chromosomes with a minus-end-directed force prior to anaphase.
source: Dynein was a good candidate for such a role since we found that it provided chromosomes with a minus-end-directed force prior to anaphase, and we observed lagging chromosomes in anaphase following dynein inhibition (Muscat et al., 2015); lagging chromosomes upon dynein depletion have also been reported by others (McNally et al., 2016) and were observed in the current study (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a discussion of previous findings and their interpretation.

claim: Lagging chromosomes were observed in anaphase following dynein inhibition.
source: Dynein was a good candidate for such a role since we found that it provided chromosomes with a minus-end-directed force prior to anaphase, and we observed lagging chromosomes in anaphase following dynein inhibition (Muscat et al., 2015); lagging chromosomes upon dynein depletion have also been reported by others (McNally et al., 2016) and were observed in the current study (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muscat et al., 2015 and McNally et al., 2016, and by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Anaphase-B-like mechanism is the major driver of chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Indeed, in subsequent years it has become clear that this anaphase-B-like mechanism is the major driver of chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes, and that anaphase A chromosome-to-pole movement provides only a minor contribution (McNally et al., 2016; Laband et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McNally et al., 2016 and Laband et al., 2017.

claim: Anaphase A chromosome-to-pole movement provides only a minor contribution to chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes.
source: Indeed, in subsequent years it has become clear that this anaphase-B-like mechanism is the major driver of chromosome segregation in C. elegans oocytes, and that anaphase A chromosome-to-pole movement provides only a minor contribution (McNally et al., 2016; Laband et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McNally et al., 2016 and Laband et al., 2017.

claim: If dynein plays a role in chromosome segregation, its contribution is redundant with other, more dominant, mechanisms.
source: Given these follow-up studies, it is now clear that if dynein plays a role in chromosome segregation, its contribution is redundant with other, more dominant, mechanisms; this would explain why most chromosomes were able to move poleward following dynein inhibition in our original study and in subsequent studies by other labs (Muscat et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2016; Laband et al., 2017; Danlasky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous studies cited.

claim: Anaphase-B-like spindle elongation can occur in the absence of KLP-18.
source: Although it is possible that KLP-18 may contribute to outward sliding of microtubules during wild-type anaphase, our work shows that this motor is not absolutely required for anaphase spindle elongation and demonstrates that there must be other factors that can perform this function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of mini anaphases in the absence of KLP-18.

claim: There must be other factors besides KLP-18 that can perform anaphase spindle elongation.
source: Although it is possible that KLP-18 may contribute to outward sliding of microtubules during wild-type anaphase, our work shows that this motor is not absolutely required for anaphase spindle elongation and demonstrates that there must be other factors that can perform this function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of mini anaphases in the absence of KLP-18.

claim: Loss of dynein activity had strong phenotypes that manifested rapidly, within 2 min of auxin treatment.
source: Our work also accentuates the importance of balanced forces within a bipolar meiotic spindle; we found that loss of dynein activity had strong phenotypes that manifested rapidly, within 2 min of auxin treatment.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from acute AID experiments.

claim: Acute dynein depletion caused spindle lengthening, suggesting that dynein may normally provide an inward force on the spindle.
source: Notably, acute dynein depletion caused spindle lengthening, suggesting that dynein may normally provide an inward force on the spindle, as has been demonstrated in previous studies of mitosis (Ferenz et al., 2009; van Heesbeen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the spindle lengthening data and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: Inactivation of KLP-18 in stable, bipolar spindles caused spindle shortening followed by collapse of microtubule minus ends into a monopolar spindle.
source: Recently, our lab also demonstrated that inactivation of KLP-18 in stable, bipolar spindles caused spindle shortening followed by collapse of microtubule minus ends into a monopolar spindle (Wolff et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolff et al., 2021.

claim: The collapse of bipolar spindles into monopolar spindles upon KLP-18 inactivation is due to a loss of the outward force provided by KLP-18.
source: This collapse is due to a loss of the outward force provided by KLP-18, theoretically enabling the inward force provided by dynein to dominate and highlighting how quickly an imbalance of these motor forces can lead to gross defects in spindle organization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings from Wolff et al., 2021.

claim: An imbalance of motor forces can quickly lead to gross defects in spindle organization.
source: This collapse is due to a loss of the outward force provided by KLP-18, theoretically enabling the inward force provided by dynein to dominate and highlighting how quickly an imbalance of these motor forces can lead to gross defects in spindle organization.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: KLP-18/kinesin-12 provides the major outward force in C. elegans oocyte meiosis.
source: While KLP-18/kinesin-12 provides the major outward force in C. elegans oocyte meiosis (Wolff et al., 2016), this critical function is performed by kinesin-5 in mouse oocytes (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007) and in mitosis in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wolff et al., 2016.

claim: Kinesin-5 provides the major outward force in mouse oocytes.
source: While KLP-18/kinesin-12 provides the major outward force in C. elegans oocyte meiosis (Wolff et al., 2016), this critical function is performed by kinesin-5 in mouse oocytes (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007) and in mitosis in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007.

claim: Kinesin-5 provides the major outward force in mitosis in many organisms.
source: While KLP-18/kinesin-12 provides the major outward force in C. elegans oocyte meiosis (Wolff et al., 2016), this critical function is performed by kinesin-5 in mouse oocytes (Schuh and Ellenberg, 2007) and in mitosis in many organisms (reviewed in Mann and Wadsworth, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Mann and Wadsworth, 2019.

claim: Dynein and kinesin-5 antagonize each other in mouse oocytes and in mitosis in many organisms.
source: Previous studies have shown that dynein and kinesin-5 antagonize each other in these organisms; inhibition of both motors simultaneously enables bipolar spindle formation (Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008; Ferenz et al., 2009; van Heesbeen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008; Ferenz et al., 2009; and van Heesbeen et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of both dynein and kinesin-5 simultaneously enables bipolar spindle formation in organisms where these motors antagonize each other.
source: Previous studies have shown that dynein and kinesin-5 antagonize each other in these organisms; inhibition of both motors simultaneously enables bipolar spindle formation (Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008; Ferenz et al., 2009; van Heesbeen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitchison et al., 2005; Tanenbaum et al., 2008; Ferenz et al., 2009; and van Heesbeen et al., 2014.

claim: Kif15/kinesin-12 is capable of providing a supplemental outward force that can support bipolarity when kinesin-5 is inhibited.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that Kif15/kinesin-12 is capable of providing a supplemental outward force that can support bipolarity when kinesin-5 is inhibited (Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009; Raaijmakers et al., 2012; Sturgill and Ohi, 2013; Sturgill et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tanenbaum et al., 2009; Vanneste et al., 2009; Raaijmakers et al., 2012; Sturgill and Ohi, 2013; and Sturgill et al., 2016.

claim: BMK-1/kinesin-5 appears to be providing a redundant outward sorting force that was only detectable once KLP-18 and dynein were removed from the meiotic spindle.
source: Here, we have provided evidence that these roles have been reversed in C. elegans oocyte meiosis; BMK-1/kinesin-5 appears to be providing a redundant outward sorting force that was only detectable once we had removed KLP-18 and dynein from the meiotic spindle.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings with bmk-1 mutants.

claim: The roles of kinesin-5 and kinesin-12 have been seemingly switched between different organisms.
source: Why the roles of kinesin-5 and kinesin-12 have been seemingly switched between different organisms is a fascinating open question.
evidence: This is a statement of an open question based on the findings.

claim: Aurora B kinase (AIR-2) is required for BMK-1 spindle localization.
source: Aurora B kinase (AIR-2) has been shown to be required for BMK-1 spindle localization and AIR-2 can phosphorylate BMK-1 in vitro (Bishop et al., 2005) implicating AIR-2 in BMK-1 regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bishop et al., 2005.

claim: AIR-2 can phosphorylate BMK-1 in vitro.
source: Aurora B kinase (AIR-2) has been shown to be required for BMK-1 spindle localization and AIR-2 can phosphorylate BMK-1 in vitro (Bishop et al., 2005) implicating AIR-2 in BMK-1 regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bishop et al., 2005.

claim: Inhibition of AIR-2's kinase activity leads to collapsed oocyte spindles.
source: Inhibition of AIR-2's kinase activity also leads to collapsed oocyte spindles (Divekar et al., 2021a), consistent with a role for AIR-2 in regulating spindle force generation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Divekar et al., 2021a.

claim: The analysis of ASPM-1 and LIN-5 provides further evidence that these proteins are directly influencing acentrosomal pole organization and stability by directing cytoplasmic dynein localization.
source: Our analysis of ASPM-1 and LIN-5 provides further evidence that these proteins are directly influencing acentrosomal pole organization and stability by directing cytoplasmic dynein localization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings with aspm-1(RNAi) and lin-5(RNAi).

claim: In either aspm-1 or lin-5 RNAi, spindle phenotypes were nearly identical to those seen in Dynein AID experimentation.
source: In either aspm-1 or lin-5 RNAi, spindle phenotypes were nearly identical to those seen in Dynein AID experimentation, and co-depletion of dynein did not worsen those phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-depletion of dynein with aspm-1 or lin-5 RNAi did not worsen the spindle phenotypes.
source: In either aspm-1 or lin-5 RNAi, spindle phenotypes were nearly identical to those seen in Dynein AID experimentation, and co-depletion of dynein did not worsen those phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The shared phenotype across depletions of ASPM-1, LIN-5, and dynein suggests that these pole proteins function in a single pathway.
source: The shared phenotype across depletions of these proteins suggests that these pole proteins function in a single pathway; this provides some credence to the concept that acentrosomal poles could contain a cross-linked network of interacting pole proteins that provide cohesion and stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Acute depletion of ZYG-9 disrupts spindle integrity in a manner that does not resemble Dynein AID depletions.
source: However, recent work from our lab has made it clear that not all pole protein depletions yield the same defects in spindle bipolarity. Acute depletion of ZYG-9, a homolog of the microtubule polymerase XMAP215, disrupts spindle integrity in a manner that does not resemble Dynein AID depletions.
evidence: This is supported by reference to recent work from the lab.

claim: Acute ZYG-9 depletion leads to an unstable multipolar spindle with defects in the middle of the spindle as well as at the poles.
source: However, acute ZYG-9 depletion leads to a unstable multipolar spindle with defects in the middle of the spindle as well as at the poles, suggesting a broader role of ZYG-9 (Mullen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mullen et al., 2022.

claim: Multiple groups of proteins are required to establish and maintain acentrosomal poles.
source: From these recent studies, it is clear that multiple groups of proteins are required to establish and maintain acentrosomal poles.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Despite having similar localizations in the meiotic spindle, pole proteins have separable functions that impact pole stability in unique ways.
source: However, despite having similar localizations in the meiotic spindle, pole proteins have separable functions that impact pole stability in unique ways.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Different groups of proteins work in parallel to form and stabilize acentrosomal poles.
source: Rather than all pole proteins interacting as a cohesive, cross-linked network around microtubule minus ends, it seems more plausible that different groups of proteins work in parallel to form and stabilize acentrosomal poles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.
